en.html:
Muramasa was not so far wrong. Translucent pillars, all interlocking in a complicated three-dimensional tangle. Call it a forest and, haan, you could see a forest.

Except forests generally put their roots in the ground. This one was floating. Botanical explanation finished there.
It reminded me of a model sailing ship, still unfinished, its bare framework exposed. Something like that was spread out below us.

In shape, at least. Give it a little more time, actually watch what it was doing, and that explanation also began to fail.

立体――確かに森と言われれば森に思える。

　地面に根を生やしておらず、宙に浮いている時点で、

　俺は帆船模型を思い出していた。完成する前、骨格

また変わる。

en.html:
...The thing was WORKING.

A strange, deep grinding sound. Like a beast gnashing its teeth far inside a cave, or a steel saw being dragged through marble. With that noise, the 'forest' shifted.

One branch split into two.
One of those joined another branch.
Something like a lump ran along the surface where they had connected.

Elsewhere, branches were retracting. A whole spreading set drew back, tip after tip, becoming one branch again—only to start growing out into some different shape.

An enormous machine. A whole factory, perhaps. That was the impression it gave me now.

...The Silver Star, meanwhile? Nothing resembling it anywhere.

en.html:
...Still. The Metal God moved, but nothing it did seemed directed at us.

Had it not noticed me? More basically, could it notice anything outside itself, choose an appropriate response, and carry it out? All this power, but was anybody at home to decide where to put it?

If it was merely a lump of energy, there was nothing to fear. Haan, a very LARGE lump. No disrespect to the quantity. But quantity alone did not make a fighter. Put enough power in one place and call it God; if the thing could not even understand that somebody was coming to break it, the grand title would not do its defending for it.

Destroying it would take work, certainly. With patience and care, though, we should be able to manage without trouble.

A sensible assessment. I was becoming quite comfortable with it.

en.html:
More than that, it did not seem to be thinking in words at all. If there was intelligence behind that voice, I would have called it very basic, very primitive.

Human arrogance, perhaps. We think in words, so naturally the whole universe must sit down and do the same, no? A mountain could stand there for ten thousand years, but ask it one question and nothing. Fail. Meanwhile a man could say 'I am a mountain' and qualify as the intelligent one. Galat answer, full marks for speaking. Very convenient examination when your own species had set the questions.

Still, for now, I could not sense a human or humanlike mind inside that 'god'.

en.html:
Whatever its reason, the gravity-wave attacks would probably continue for as long as we stayed here. And leaving was not an option now.

...Dodging them was not actually so difficult.

You could see the preparation before each shot. Its aim was poor. Instead of carefully predicting our movements, it seemed to be firing more or less anyhow. Pay attention and the attacks were easy to read.

The power behind them, though. Arre.
I was leaving such a generous margin that anyone watching might have called me a coward. Let them. Even at that distance, the aftershock travelling through space shook my whole body.

A direct hit? Muramasa was probably entirely correct about that.

Perhaps we had a ninety-percent chance of success. Very encouraging number—until the other ten percent came to collect. The price of that failure was far too high.
Finish this quickly. As quickly as we possibly could.

The great form of that 'god' was indeed damaged. Part of its crystal forest looked as though the worst sort of logging contractor had been let loose in it.

I thought we had hurt it badly. The scream certainly went on and on. If Muramasa had not been suppressing it, I would probably have been writhing with both hands over my ears.

　現に〝神〟の悲鳴は長く尾を引き、もし村正が抑制
してくれていなかったら俺は両耳を押さえてのたうち
回っていたことだろう。
